verses.32:9: it is not the long-lived who are wise, nor do the aged know judgment.'
verses.32:10: Therefore I said, 'Listen to me, and I will declare to you what I know.'
verses.32:11: Give ear to my words while you listen, until you examine arguments;
verses.32:12: and even to you I will pay attention. And look, there was no one refuting Job, answering back his words, from among you,
verses.32:13: so that you may not say, 'We have found wisdom by joining ourselves to the Lord';
verses.32:14: yet you permitted a man to speak such words.
verses.32:15: They were dismayed; they did not answer any longer; they made arguments grow old away from them.
verses.32:16: I waited, for I did not speak, because they stood still; they did not answer."
verses.32:18: "I will speak again, for I am full of words; for the spirit of my belly is destroying me;
verses.32:19: and my belly is like a skin of new wine, fermenting and tied shut, or like a coppersmith's bellows that has burst.
verses.32:20: I will speak so that I may find relief, opening my lips;
verses.32:21: for I will certainly not feel shame before a man, nor indeed will I defer to a mortal;
verses.32:22: for I do not know how to admire persons; otherwise, moths will eat me too."
verses.33:1: "Nevertheless, hear my words, Job, and give ear to my speech;
verses.33:2: for look, I have opened my mouth, and my tongue has spoken.
verses.33:3: My heart is pure in words, and the understanding of my lips will perceive pure things.
verses.33:4: It is the divine spirit that made me, and the breath of the Almighty that teaches me.
verses.33:5: If you are able, give me an answer to these things; hold firm, stand opposite me, and I opposite you.
verses.33:6: From clay you have been formed, just as I also have; from the same we have been formed.
verses.33:7: Fear of me will not unsettle you, nor will my hand be heavy upon you.
verses.33:8: Yet you spoke in my ears; I have heard the sound of words;
verses.33:9: because you say, 'I am pure, not having sinned; I am blameless, for I did not act lawlessly;
verses.33:10: yet He found a complaint against me, and He has regarded me as an adversary;
verses.33:11: and He put my foot in the stocks, and He watched all my paths.'
verses.33:12: For how do you say, 'I am righteous, and He has not listened to me'? For the One who is above mortals is eternal.
verses.33:13: And you say, 'Why has He not listened to me in any word of my case?'
verses.33:14: For once the Lord may speak, and a second time,
verses.33:15: in a dream, or in a night meditation, as when dreadful fear falls upon men, during slumbers upon a bed;
verses.33:16: then He uncovers the mind of men; with such visions of fear He terrifies them,
verses.33:17: to turn a man away from unrighteousness; and He rescues his body from a fall.
verses.33:18: And He spares his soul from death, and spares him from falling in war.
verses.33:19: Again He reproves him in sickness upon a bed, and the multitude of his bones grows numb;
verses.33:20: and he will certainly not be able to accept any food of grain, and his soul will desire food,
verses.33:21: until his flesh decays and he shows his bones empty.
verses.33:22: And his soul draws near to death; this life of his is in Hades.
verses.33:23: If there are a thousand death-bringing angels, not one of them will by any means wound him. If he intends in his heart to turn back to the Lord, and declares to a man his own fault, and shows his folly,
verses.33:24: He will uphold him so that he does not fall into death; and He will renew his body like plaster on a wall, and He will fill his bones with marrow;
verses.33:25: and He will make his flesh tender like that of an infant, and He will restore him, grown to manhood, among men.
verses.33:26: And when he has prayed to the Lord, it will be acceptable to Him, and he will enter with a cheerful face, with confession; and He will render righteousness to men.
verses.33:27: Then at that time a man will reproach himself, saying, 'What sorts of things was I doing? And He did not punish me as what I sinned deserved.
verses.33:28: Save my soul from coming into corruption, and my life will see light.'
verses.33:29: Look, the Mighty One will work all these things three ways with a man;
verses.33:30: but He rescued my soul from death, so that my life may praise Him in light.
verses.33:31: Give ear, Job, and listen to me; be silent, and it is I who will speak.
verses.33:32: If there is a word, answer me; speak, for I want you to be justified.
verses.33:33: If not, you listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you."
verses.34:2: "Hear me, you who are wise; you who have knowledge, give ear;
verses.34:3: for the ear tests words, and the throat tastes food.
verses.34:4: Let us choose judgment for ourselves; let us know among ourselves what is good.
verses.34:5: For Job has said, 'I am righteous; the Lord has taken away my judgment,
verses.34:6: and He has dealt falsely with my judgment; violent is my arrow without injustice.'
verses.34:7: What man is like Job, drinking mockery like water,
verses.34:8: not having sinned nor acted ungodly, or having shared a way with those who do lawless deeds, to walk with the ungodly?
verses.34:9: For do not say, 'There will be no visitation of a man,' when there is visitation for him from the Lord.
verses.34:10: Therefore, you of understanding heart, hear me: Far be it from me to act ungodly before the Lord, and before the Almighty to disturb what is right;
verses.34:11: but He repays a person according to what each of them does, and in the path of a man He will find him.
verses.34:12: Now do you suppose that the Lord will do wrong things? Or will the Almighty disturb judgment,
verses.34:13: He who made the earth? And who is the one who makes what is under heaven and all the things in it?
verses.34:14: For if He should wish to hold back, and to retain the spirit with Himself,
verses.34:15: all flesh will die together, and every mortal will depart to the earth from where he was also formed.
verses.34:16: But if you are not admonished, hear these things; give ear to the sound of words.
verses.34:17: You, look at the One who hates lawless deeds and the One who destroys the wicked, who is eternally righteous.
verses.34:18: Ungodly is the one who says to a king, 'You act lawlessly'; 'Most ungodly one,' to rulers,
verses.34:19: who is not ashamed before the face of an honored man, nor knows how to grant honor to the great, so that their faces might be admired.
verses.34:20: And crying out and pleading with a man will turn out in vain for them; for they acted lawlessly, while the powerless were turned aside.
verses.34:21: For He Himself is an observer of the works of people, and nothing of what they do escapes His notice;
verses.34:22: nor will there be a place for those who do lawless deeds to be hidden;
verses.34:23: for He will lay no more upon a man.
verses.34:24: For the Lord watches over all, the One who comprehends unsearchable things, both glorious and marvelous things, of which there is no number,
verses.34:25: the One who knows their works; and He will overturn the night, and it will be brought low.
verses.34:26: And He extinguished the ungodly, and they are visible before Him,
verses.34:27: because they turned aside from the law of God, and they did not acknowledge His ordinances,
verses.34:28: so as to bring to Him the cry of the needy, and He will hear the cry of the poor.
verses.34:29: And He Himself will grant quietness, and who will condemn? And He will hide His face, and who will see Him? Both over a nation and over a man alike,
verses.34:30: making a hypocritical man king because of the perversity of the people.
verses.34:31: For there is one who says to the Mighty One, 'I have received; I will not take a pledge;
verses.34:32: apart from myself I will see; You show me; if I have done injustice, I will by no means add to it.'
verses.34:33: Will He repay it from you, because you will reject it? For you will choose, and not I; and what you know, speak.
verses.34:34: Therefore those of understanding heart will say these things, and a wise man has heard my word.
verses.34:35: But Job did not speak with understanding; his words are not with knowledge.
verses.34:36: Nevertheless, learn, Job: do not give a reply any longer like the foolish,
verses.34:37: so that we may not add to our sins; and lawlessness will be counted against us when we speak many words before the Lord."
verses.35:2: "What is this you have considered in judgment? Who are you that you said, 'I am righteous before the Lord'?
verses.35:4: I will give an answer to you and to your three friends.
verses.35:5: Look up to heaven and see, and observe the clouds, how high they are above you.
verses.35:6: If you have sinned, what will you do? And even if you have committed many lawless deeds, what can you do?
verses.35:7: And since, then, you are righteous, what will you give to Him, or what will He receive from your hand?
verses.35:8: Your ungodliness is for a man like yourself, and your righteousness is for a son of man.
verses.35:9: Because of a multitude, those who are oppressed will cry out; they will shout because of the arm of many.
verses.35:10: And no one said, 'Where is God who made me, who appoints night watches,
verses.35:11: who distinguishes me from the four-footed animals of the earth, and from the birds of heaven?'
verses.35:12: There they will cry out, and He will by no means hear, also because of the arrogance of the wicked.
verses.35:13: For the Lord does not wish to see wrong things; for the Almighty Himself is an observer
verses.35:14: of those who carry out lawless deeds, and He will save me. Now be judged before Him, if you can praise Him as He is.
verses.35:15: And now, because He is not visiting His wrath, and He has not taken much notice of any trespass,
verses.35:16: Job also opens his mouth in vain; in ignorance he makes words heavy."
verses.36:2: "Wait for me a little longer so that I may teach you, for there is still speech in me.
verses.36:3: Taking up my knowledge from afar, and by my works I will speak righteous things in truth,
verses.36:4: and not unrighteous words; you understand unrighteously.
verses.36:5: But know that the Lord will by no means reject the innocent; powerful in strength of heart,
verses.36:6: He will by no means keep an ungodly person alive, and He will give justice to the poor.
verses.36:7: He will not take away His eyes from the righteous, and with kings on a throne He will indeed seat them to victory, and they will be exalted.
verses.36:8: And those who have been bound in manacles will be held fast in cords of poverty;
verses.36:9: and He will declare to them their works and their transgressions, because they will grow strong.
verses.36:10: But He will listen to the righteous, and He said that they will turn back from unrighteousness.
verses.36:11: If they listen and serve, they will complete their days in good things, and their years in splendor.
verses.36:12: But He does not save the ungodly, because they are unwilling to know the Lord, and because, when admonished, they were disobedient.
verses.36:13: And hypocrites in heart will appoint wrath; they will not cry out, because He bound them.
verses.36:14: May their soul therefore die in youth, and may their life be wounded by angels,
verses.36:15: because they afflicted the weak and the powerless; but He will set forth the justice of the meek.
verses.36:16: And an abyss deceived you even further out of the mouth of an enemy, a pouring down beneath it, and your table went down full of fatness.
verses.36:17: And justice will not be lacking from the righteous,
verses.36:18: but wrath will be upon the ungodly, because of the ungodliness of gifts that they were receiving for acts of unrighteousness.
verses.36:19: Do not let your mind willingly turn you aside from the plea of the powerless who are in distress,
verses.36:20: and all those who exert strength. Do not draw out the night, for peoples to go up in their place;
verses.36:21: but guard yourself that you do not do unrighteous things; for you made your choice for this rather than poverty.
verses.36:22: Look, the Mighty One will prevail in His strength; for who is a ruler like Him?
verses.36:23: And who is the one who examines His works? Or who is the one who said, 'He did unrighteous things'?
verses.36:24: Remember that His works are great, over which men ruled;
verses.36:25: every person has seen within himself, all who are wounded mortals.
verses.36:26: Look, the Mighty One is great, and we will not know; the number of His years is also boundless.
verses.36:27: Yet the drops of rain are numbered by Him, and they will be poured out in rain into a cloud;
verses.36:28: ancient things will flow, and clouds cast shade over countless mortals. He appointed a season for the animals, and they know the order of a resting place. At all these things, is your understanding not astonished, nor is your heart separated from your body?
verses.36:29: And if one understands the spreadings of a cloud, the equality of His tent,
verses.36:30: look, the song will extend over Him, and He covered the roots of the sea.
verses.36:31: For by them He will judge peoples; He will give food to the one who listens.
verses.36:32: Upon hands He covered light, and He commanded concerning it upon one who comes to meet;
verses.36:33: He will declare His friend concerning it; the Lord is a possession, even concerning unrighteousness."
verses.37:1: "At this also my heart was troubled and slipped away from its place.
verses.37:2: Hear a sound in the anger of the wrath of the Lord, and meditation will go out from His mouth.
verses.37:3: Beneath the whole heaven is His dominion, and His light is upon the wings of the earth.
verses.37:4: After it He will cry out with a voice; He will thunder with the voice of His pride, and He will not exchange them, because you will hear His voice.
verses.37:5: The Mighty One will thunder wondrous things with His voice, for He has done great things that we did not know,
verses.37:6: commanding the snow, 'Be on the earth,' and a storm of rain, and a storm of the rains of His power.
verses.37:7: He sets a seal on the hand of every person, so that every person may know his own weakness.
verses.37:8: And wild beasts entered under shelter, and they grew still in a resting place.
verses.37:9: Out of chambers pains come, and from summits, cold.
verses.37:10: And from the breath of the Mighty One He will give frost, and He steers the water however He wishes;
verses.37:11: and a cloud covers over what is choice. A cloud will scatter His light.
verses.37:12: And He Himself will turn the circuits in theeboulathoth for their works; all that He commands them, these things have been ordered by Him upon the earth,
verses.37:13: whether for discipline, whether for His earth, whether for mercy, He will find him.
verses.37:14: Give ear to these things, Job; stand still, being admonished concerning the power of the Lord.
verses.37:15: We know that God appointed His works, having made light out of darkness.
verses.37:16: And He understands the separation of clouds, and the extraordinary downfalls of the wicked.
verses.37:17: And your robe is warm, and it is quiet upon the earth.
verses.37:18: You will make firm with Him for ancient things, strong as the appearance of an outpouring.
verses.37:19: Why? Teach me what we will say to Him, and let us stop saying many things.
verses.37:20: Does a book or a scribe stand beside me, so that, standing, I should silence a person?
verses.37:21: And the light is not visible to all; it is radiant in the ancient things, just like that which is from Him upon clouds.
verses.37:22: From the north, clouds gleaming with gold; upon these, great is the glory and honor of the Almighty.
verses.37:23: And we do not find another equal to His strength; the One who judges righteous things, do you not think that He listens?
verses.37:24: Therefore people will fear Him, and the wise in heart will also fear Him."
verses.38:1: Now after Elihu stopped speaking, the Lord said to Job through a whirlwind and clouds:
verses.38:2: "Who is this who hides counsel from Me, and holds back words in his heart, and thinks he hides them from Me?
verses.38:3: Gird your loins like a man; I will ask, and you answer Me.
verses.38:4: Where were you when I founded the earth? And declare to Me, if you know understanding.
verses.38:5: Who set its measurements, if you know? Or who is the one who drew a cord over it?
verses.38:6: Upon what are its rings fixed? And who is the one who laid a cornerstone upon it?
verses.38:7: When stars came into being, all My angels praised Me with a loud voice.
verses.38:8: And I enclosed the sea with gates, when it surged violently as it came forth from a mother's womb;
verses.38:9: and I set a cloud as its clothing, and with mist I swaddled it;
verses.38:10: and I set boundaries for it, placing bars and gates around it;
verses.38:11: and I said to it, 'Up to this point you will come, and you will not pass beyond, but within yourself your waves will be shattered.'
verses.38:12: Or in your time have I commanded the morning light, and did the morning star see its own station,
verses.38:13: to take hold of the wings of the earth, to shake the ungodly out of it?
verses.38:14: Or did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set him upon the earth able to speak?
verses.38:15: And have you taken away the light from the ungodly, and shattered the arm of the arrogant?
verses.38:16: And have you come to the spring of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss?
verses.38:17: And do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?
verses.38:18: And have you been instructed about the breadth of what is under heaven? Report to Me now just how large it is.
verses.38:19: And in what land does the light lodge, and what is the place of darkness?
verses.38:20: Could you lead Me to their boundaries? And do you also know their paths?
verses.38:21: I know, then, that you were born at that time, and the number of your years is great.
verses.38:22: And have you come to the treasuries of snow, and have you seen the treasuries of hail?
verses.38:23: And is it stored up for you for an hour of enemies, for a day of wars and battle?
verses.38:24: And from where does frost come forth, or is the south wind scattered over what is under heaven?
verses.38:25: And who prepared a course for a violent rain, and a way of tumults,
verses.38:26: to send rain upon a land where there is no man, a wilderness in which no human being exists,
verses.38:27: to satisfy what is untrodden and uninhabited, and to make an outgrowth of tender grass sprout?
verses.38:28: Who is the father of rain? And who is the one who has given birth to clods of dew?
verses.38:29: And from whose womb does the ice come forth? And who has given birth to frost in heaven,
verses.38:30: which comes down like flowing water? And who has terrified the face of an ungodly person?
verses.38:31: And have you understood the bond of the Pleiades, and have you opened the enclosure of Orion?
verses.38:32: Or will you open up Mazuroth in its season, and Hesperus by its hair, will you lead them?
verses.38:33: And do you know the turnings of heaven, or the things under heaven that take place in unison?
verses.38:34: And will you call a cloud with a voice, and will it obey you with a violent trembling of water?
verses.38:35: And will you send out thunderbolts, and will they go? And will they say to you, 'What is it?'
verses.38:36: And who gave women wisdom of weaving, or knowledge of embroidery?
verses.38:37: And who is the one who counts clouds in wisdom, and bent heaven to the earth?
verses.38:38: And dust has been poured out like earth, and I have bonded it like a cube to a stone.
verses.38:39: And will you hunt prey for lions, and fill the souls of dragons?
verses.38:40: For they are afraid in their dens, and they sit in thickets lying in ambush.
verses.38:41: And who prepared prey for a raven? For its young cry out to the Lord, wandering about seeking food."
verses.39:1: "Do you know the time of birth of goat-stags of the rock, and have you watched the birth pangs of deer?
verses.39:2: And have you counted their months full for birth, and have you loosed their birth pangs?
verses.39:3: And have you raised their little ones apart from fear? Will you send away their birth pangs?
verses.39:4: Their offspring will break away, they will multiply in produce; they will go out, and they will by no means return to them.
verses.39:5: And who is the one who let a wild donkey go free, and who loosed its bonds?
verses.39:6: And I made its habitation a wilderness, and its dwellings a salt land.
verses.39:7: Laughing at the throng of a city, and not hearing the reproach of a tax collector,
verses.39:8: it will survey mountains, its pasture, and it seeks after every green thing.
verses.39:9: And will a unicorn be willing to serve you, or to sleep at your manger?
verses.39:10: And will you bind its yoke with straps, or will it draw your furrows in a plain?
verses.39:11: And do you trust in it because its strength is great, and will you leave your works to it?
verses.39:12: And will you believe that it will return the seed to you, and bring in your threshing floor?
verses.39:13: A wing of those who delight, if hasida and nessa conceive;
verses.39:14: for she will leave her eggs on the ground, and warm them on the dust;
verses.39:15: and they forgot that a foot will scatter them, and wild beasts of the field will trample them.
verses.39:16: She treated her own children harshly, so as not herself; in vain she labored without fear.
verses.39:17: For God kept wisdom silent from her, and did not share with her in understanding.
verses.39:18: At the right time she will rise on high; she will laugh at a horse and its rider.
verses.39:19: Or did you place strength upon a horse, and clothe its neck with fear?
verses.39:20: And did you array it with full armor, and the glory of its chest with boldness?
verses.39:21: Digging in a plain, it exults, and it goes forth into a plain in strength;
verses.39:22: Meeting a king, it laughs, and it will by no means turn back from iron.
verses.39:23: Upon it a bow and a sword exult,
verses.39:24: and in anger it will make the ground vanish; and it will by no means believe until a trumpet sounds.
verses.39:25: And when a trumpet sounds, it says, 'Well done!' And from a distance it scents war with a leap and a shout.
verses.39:26: And by your knowledge does a hawk stand, having spread out its wings motionless, looking down on what lies to the south?
verses.39:27: And at your command does an eagle rise high, and does a vulture, sitting upon its nest, lodge
verses.39:28: upon a crag of rock and in a hidden place?
verses.39:29: Being there, it seeks food; from a distance its eyes keep watch;
verses.39:30: and its young wallow in blood, and wherever the dead are, immediately they are found."
verses.40:1: And the Lord God answered Job and said,
verses.40:2: "Will anyone turn aside judgment with the Sufficient One? And will one who reproves God answer it?"
verses.40:3: Then Job answered and said to the Lord,
verses.40:4: "Why do I still contend in judgment, being admonished and reproving the Lord, hearing such things when I am nothing? And what answer will I give to these things? I will put my hand over my mouth.
verses.40:5: I have spoken once, and I will not continue a second time."
verses.40:6: Then the Lord, responding further, said to Job out of the cloud,
verses.40:7: "No, rather gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you answer Me.
verses.40:8: Do not reject My judgment. And do you suppose that I have dealt with you otherwise than that you might appear righteous?
verses.40:9: Or do you have an arm against the Lord, or do you thunder with a voice against Him?
verses.40:10: Now take up loftiness and power, and clothe yourself with glory and honor.
verses.40:11: And send out angels in wrath, and humble every insolent one,
verses.40:12: and extinguish the proud one; and make the ungodly rot immediately,
verses.40:13: and hide them in the earth all together, and fill their faces with dishonor;
verses.40:14: I will acknowledge that your right hand is able to save.
verses.40:15: But now, look, wild beasts are beside you; they eat grass just like oxen.
verses.40:16: Look now, its strength is in its loins, and its power is in the navel of its belly.
verses.40:17: It sets its tail upright like a cypress, and its sinews are intertwined.
verses.40:18: Its ribs are bronze ribs, and its backbone is cast iron.
verses.40:19: This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by His angels.
verses.40:20: And going up onto a sheer mountain, it causes joy for four-footed creatures in Tartarus.
verses.40:21: It sleeps under all kinds of trees, beside papyrus and reed and sedge.
verses.40:22: And great trees with shoots, and branches of the field, are shaded by it.
verses.40:23: If a flood happens, it will by no means notice; it is confident that the Jordan will dash into its mouth.
verses.40:24: Will one take it in its eye? Acting craftily, will one pierce its nose?
verses.40:25: And will you lead a dragon with a hook, and put a halter around its nose?
verses.40:26: Will you tie a ring in its nostril, and pierce its lip with a bracelet?
verses.40:27: And will it speak to you with a plea, softly with supplication?
verses.40:28: Will it make a covenant with you? And will you take it as a perpetual servant?
verses.40:29: And will you play with it like a bird, or will you tie it like a sparrow for a child?
verses.40:30: And do nations feed on it, and do nations of the Phoenicians divide it up?
verses.40:31: And all sailing vessels coming together will by no means carry one hide of its tail, or its head in fishermen's boats.
verses.40:32: And one will lay a hand on it, remembering the battle that takes place in its body."
verses.41:1: "Have you not even marveled at the things being said?
verses.41:2: Do you not even fear because it has been prepared for Me? For who is the one who has stood against Me?
verses.41:3: Or who will stand against Me and endure? If all that is under heaven is Mine,
verses.41:4: I will not be silent because of it, and concerning a word of power, it will have mercy on its equal.
verses.41:5: Who will uncover the face of its garment? And who could enter into the fold of its breastplate?
verses.41:6: Who will open the gates of its face? Around its teeth is terror.
verses.41:7: Its inward parts are bronze shields; its bond is like an emery stone.
verses.41:8: One clings to another, and air will by no means pass through it.
verses.41:9: Each one will cling to his brother; they hold together, and they will by no means be torn apart.
verses.41:10: In its sneezing, light flashes forth, and its eyes are the appearance of the morning star.
verses.41:11: Out of its mouth go burning torches, and braziers of fire are flung about.
verses.41:12: Out of its nostrils goes the smoke of a furnace burning with a fire of coals.
verses.41:13: Its soul is coals, and a flame goes out of its mouth.
verses.41:14: And power lodges in its neck; destruction runs before it.
verses.41:15: And the fleshy parts of its body cling together. One pours down upon it; it will not be shaken.
verses.41:16: Its heart is hardened like a stone, and it stands like an unyielding anvil.
verses.41:17: And when it turns, there is terror for four-footed wild beasts leaping on the earth.
verses.41:18: If lances meet it, they will accomplish nothing: spear and breastplate.
verses.41:19: For it regards iron as chaff, and bronze like rotten wood.
verses.41:20: A bronze bow will by no means wound it; it regards a catapult as grass,
verses.41:21: hammers are counted like stubble, and it laughs at the shaking of a fire-bearer.
verses.41:22: Its bed is sharp spikes, and all the gold of the sea under it is like untold mud.
verses.41:23: It makes the abyss boil like a bronze cauldron; and it regards the sea like an ointment pot,
verses.41:24: and the Tartarus of the abyss like a captive; it counts the abyss as a walkway.
verses.41:25: There is nothing on the earth like it, made to be mocked by My angels.
verses.41:26: It sees everything lofty, and it itself is king of all those in the waters."
verses.42:1: Then Job answered and said to the Lord,
verses.42:2: "I know that You are able to do all things, and nothing is impossible for You.
verses.42:3: For who is the one who hides counsel from You? And holding back words, does he think to hide even from You? And who will declare to me what I did not know, great and marvelous things that I did not understand?
verses.42:4: Now hear me, Lord, so that I also may speak; I will ask, and You teach me.
verses.42:5: With the hearing of the ear I heard of You formerly, but now my eye has seen You.
verses.42:6: Therefore I held myself in contempt and wasted away, and I have regarded myself as earth and ashes."
verses.42:7: And it happened, after the Lord had spoken all these words to Job, that the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "You have sinned, you and your friends; for you have spoken nothing true before Me, as My servant Job has.
verses.42:8: Now then, take seven calves and seven rams, and go to My servant Job, and he will offer burnt offerings on your behalf. And Job, My servant, will pray for you, for I will accept only his face; for had it not been for him, I would have destroyed you; for you have not spoken what is true against My servant Job."
verses.42:9: So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Minaean went and did just as the Lord had commanded them; and He pardoned their sin because of Job.
verses.42:10: And the Lord made Job great; and when he prayed also for his friends, He forgave them their sin; and the Lord gave twice as much as all that belonged to Job before, in double measure.
verses.42:11: And all his brothers and his sisters heard all the things that had happened to him, and came to him, along with all who had known him from the first. And after eating and drinking with him, they comforted him and marveled at all that the Lord had brought upon him; and each one gave him one ewe lamb and a tetradrachm of gold, unstamped.
verses.42:12: And the Lord blessed the latter days of Job more than the former; and his livestock were fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and one thousand grazing female donkeys.
verses.42:13: And seven sons and three daughters were born to him.
verses.42:14: And he named the first Day, and the second Cassia, and the third Horn of Amalthea.
verses.42:15: And none were found comparable to the daughters of Job, better than they, in the earth under heaven; and their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
verses.42:16: And Job lived after the affliction one hundred and seventy years, and all the years he lived were two hundred and forty; and Job saw his sons and the sons of his sons, the fourth generation.
verses.42:17: And Job died, old and full of days. And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises up. This man is explained from the Syriac book as dwelling in the land of Uz, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia; and previously his name was Jobab. And having taken an Arabian wife, he fathered a son whose name was Ennon; and he himself was born of his father Zerah, a son from the sons of Esau, and of his mother Bozrah, so that he was fifth from Abraham. And these are the kings who reigned in Edom, the country over which he himself also ruled: first, Balak the son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dinhabah; and after Balak, Jobab, who is called Job; and after him, Husham, who was governor from the Temanite country; and after him, Hadad the son of Barad, who cut down Midian in the plain of Moab, and the name of his city was Getthaim. And the friends who came to him were Eliphaz, of the sons of Esau, king of the Temanites; Bildad, the ruler of the Shuhites; Zophar, the king of the Minaeans.

notes.1:1: Greek reads "in the land of Ausitis," the Septuagint geographical form corresponding to Hebrew Uz.
notes.1:6: Greek "the angels of God" corresponds to Hebrew "sons of God," and "the devil" (ho diabolos, literally "the slanderer") renders Hebrew ha-satan ("the adversary").
notes.1:11: Greek "he will bless You" preserves the traditional euphemism for cursing God (so also in 2:5).
notes.1:15: Greek "the captors" here and "the horsemen" in 1:17 are distinctive Septuagint readings where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "the Sabeans" and "the Chaldeans."
notes.1:21: The clause "as it seemed good to the Lord, so it came to be" is a Septuagint reading not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (compare also the explicit sin-offering calf added in 1:5).
notes.2:3: Greek reads "yet you said to destroy his possessions without cause," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "though you incited Me against him to destroy him without cause."
notes.2:8: Greek specifies scraping away "the discharge" (ichor) and places Job "on the dung heap outside the city," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "among the ashes."
notes.2:9: The Septuagint preserves a substantially longer lament by Job's wife than the Hebrew Masoretic Text, concluding with "speak some word against the Lord, and die."
notes.2:11: The Septuagint gives royal titles to Job's friends (calling Bildad tyrannos, "ruler") and uniquely identifies Zophar as king of the Minaeans rather than the Hebrew Naamathite.
notes.3:8: Greek "the great sea monster" (to mega ketos) renders Hebrew Leviathan, and "to subdue" contrasts with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "to rouse up."
notes.3:14: Greek "who gloried in swords" reflects a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonantal text behind the Masoretic reading "who rebuilt ruins."
notes.3:17: Greek "have kindled the fury of wrath" differs sharply from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "cease from troubling."
notes.3:18: Greek "the eternal ones" (hoi aionioi, the dead of ages past) and "tax collector" stand where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "prisoners" and "taskmaster"; in 3:19 Greek likewise reads "a servant who fears his master" rather than "free from his master."
notes.3:23: The Septuagint reads "Death is rest for a man" in place of the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "to a man whose way is hidden."
notes.4:6: The Greek diverges sharply from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, rendering Job's fear as "in folly" and referring to "the wickedness of your way" rather than his confidence and integrity.
notes.4:11: Greek myrmekoleon literally denotes an "ant-lion," a legendary hybrid beast in ancient Greek lore; similarly, v. 10 reads "dragons" (drakonton) where the Hebrew refers to young lions.
notes.4:12: The Greek conditional sentence replaces the Hebrew opening about a stealthy word; "from Him" (par' autou) naturally refers to the Lord (cf. v. 9; 5:9), though some take it to refer to the preceding "word" ("from it").
notes.4:17: The Greek reads "from his works" (apo ton ergon autou) rather than the Hebrew "than his Maker."
notes.4:19: The Greek uniquely shifts to the first-person plural ("we ourselves also are from the same clay"), favoring closing the disembodied voice's quotation at v. 17, though many interpreters extend the voice's speech through v. 21.
notes.5:4: Greek kolabristheiesan is a rare verb denoting mocking or humiliating treatment, and the Greek specifies "at the doors of inferiors" rather than the Hebrew "in the gate."
notes.5:5: Greek eksiphonistheie is a rare verb meaning literally "may it be siphoned out" or "drained dry."
notes.5:7: The Greek renders the second clause with "the young of a vulture" (neossoi gypos) rather than the Hebrew "sparks" (lit. "sons of Resheph"), just as v. 6 reads "from the mountains."
notes.5:24: Greek diaita can mean "dwelling" (as in v. 3) or "way of life," and hamarte literally means "miss the mark," "fail," or "sin."
notes.5:27: Unlike the shorter Hebrew ending ("know it for yourself"), the Greek adds the pointed accusation "if you have done anything" (ei ti epraxas); similarly, v. 23 lacks the Hebrew clause about a covenant with the stones of the field.
notes.6:7: Greek bromon (a Koine spelling of bromos, 'stench') pairs with osmen ('smell'), giving a distinctive Septuagint reading in which Job's anger cannot cease and his food appears as a stench like a lion's odor.
notes.6:9: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, where Job asks God to cut him off, the Greek includes the negative particle me ('yet let Him not destroy me completely').
notes.6:10: The Greek presents distinctive imagery ('may my city be a grave, upon whose walls I used to leap') and renders the following clause as Job affirming he has not lied about God's holy words.
notes.6:19: Greek Thaimanon ('Temanites') and Sabon ('Sabeans') are plural ethnic names; 'Temanites' preserves a distinct Septuagint reading compared with the singular place name Tema in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:5: Greek ichoros denotes the watery fluid or discharge oozing from sores, vividly depicting Job dissolving clods of earth with this discharge as he scrapes himself.
notes.7:6: Greek elaphroteros lalias ('swifter than speech', or 'lighter than speech') reflects a Septuagint reading distinct from the weaver's shuttle imagery of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:15: The Greek reads a 2nd-person future statement addressed to God ('You will separate my soul from my spirit, and my bones from death'), diverging markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:18: Greek eis anapausin ('until rest', or 'for rest') pairs temporally with 'until the morning', reflecting the sense 'rest' rather than 'moment' as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:20: Greek katenteukten ('accuser') is a rare compound noun meaning one who lodges a complaint against another, and epi soi ('to You') preserves a reading differing from 'to myself' in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.8:12: Greek reads "before drinking, does not every plant dry up?" (pro tou piein), diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("before any other grass it withers").
notes.8:14: Greek reads "his house will be uninhabited" (aoiketos), diverging from the Hebrew ("his confidence is cut off"); the noun arachne ("spider") denotes a spider's web here.
notes.8:16: Greek reads "out of his decay" (ek saprias autou, also "rottenness"), diverging from the Hebrew ("over his garden").
notes.8:18: The Greek verb katapie ("swallows up") has no explicit subject or object, and the final clause reads "you have not seen such things" rather than direct speech from the place ("I have never seen you").
notes.9:3: The unexpressed third-person subjects and pronouns in Greek are ambiguous; the second and third clauses can also be read with God as the subject who refuses to heed the mortal or reply to one of his words.
notes.9:9: Greek preserves the distinctive astronomical names Hesperus (the evening star, where Hebrew has Orion) and Arcturus (where Hebrew has the Bear).
notes.9:13: Unlike the Hebrew ("God will not turn back his anger"), the Greek text lacks a negation ("He Himself has turned away anger") and renders "the helpers of Rahab" as "the sea monsters under heaven" (kete).
notes.9:24: Greek has plural "they have been handed over" (referring to the righteous in 9:23) rather than Hebrew "the earth is given," while retaining the feminine singular pronoun "its" (autes) in "its judges."
notes.9:33: Greek expresses an unattainable wish, "If only there were" (eithe en), rather than the Hebrew negative statement ("there is not").
notes.10:1: The Greek opens with a participial phrase ("being weary in my soul") punctuated as an independent clause, which in some Greek editions is linked either to 9:35 or to the following participle "groaning."
notes.10:2: The Septuagint reads "Do not teach me to act ungodly" rather than the Masoretic Hebrew "Do not condemn me."
notes.10:3: Greek "if I act unjustly" (adikeso) is first person, unlike the Hebrew; apeipo is read as second-person aorist middle ("You have renounced"), parallel to prosesches ("You have paid attention").
notes.10:17: Greek peirateria refers primarily to "raiding bands" (marauders) and can also carry the sense of "trials" or "ordeals"; etasis denotes a judicial examination or scrutiny.
notes.10:18: The Greek uses simple aorist indicatives ("and I did not die, and no eye saw me, and I became" in 10:18-19) following "Why...?" to express the unrealized outcome Job wished had happened at birth.
notes.11:1: The Septuagint identifies Zophar as "the Minaean" (Greek ho Meinaios, referring to the Minaeans of Arabia) rather than the Hebrew "Naamathite."
notes.11:3: The opening beatitude ("Blessed is the short-lived one born of a woman") is a distinctive Septuagint reading with no direct counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.11:6: The Greek literally states "for He will be double of the things concerning you," and the following clause asserts that what has come upon Job from the Lord is worthy of his sins (unlike the Hebrew, which speaks of God exacting less than guilt deserves).
notes.11:12: Literally "a man swims idly in words" (allos nechetai logois), a vivid Septuagint rendering distinct from the Hebrew proverb about an empty man gaining understanding.
notes.12:5: Verses 12:4-6 in the Septuagint present a substantially different line of thought from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, emphasizing the plundering of the righteous man and the certainty of an examination of the wicked.
notes.12:10: The Greek begins literally with ei me ("if not" or "unless"), functioning here as an emphatic rhetorical question ("Is not...?").
notes.12:11: The Greek reads nous ("mind") rather than ous ("ear"), and larynx ("throat") for the organ of taste.
notes.12:18: Throughout 12:17-24, the Greek pairs present participles with gnomic aorists (rendered here in the timeless present) and preserves distinctive Septuagint readings such as "seats kings upon thrones" (12:18), "knows the understanding of the elders" (12:20), and "heals the humble" (12:21).
notes.12:25: Both verbs in the Greek are in the optative mood, expressing a wish ("May they grope... and may they wander astray") rather than a simple indicative statement.
notes.13:3: The Greek qualifies Job's resolve to argue before the Lord with the third-person condition "if He wills" (ἐὰν βούληται), whereas the Hebrew expresses Job's own desire to argue with God.
notes.13:9: The Greek speaks of going to all lengths to attach oneself to God (προστεθήσεσθε αὐτῷ), diverging from the Hebrew comparison to deceiving a human.
notes.13:15: In a notable divergence from the Hebrew ("Though he slay me, I will hope in him"), the Greek affirms that even if the Mighty One overpowers Job, since He has already begun, Job will surely speak and argue before Him.
notes.13:22: In the Greek, God is the subject of both "call" and "speak" and Job responds in both clauses, unlike the Hebrew where Job speaks in the second half.
notes.13:28: The neuter relative pronoun "which" (ὃ) refers back loosely to Job's bodily condition, and the Greek compares it to a "wineskin" (ἀσκῷ) rather than a rotten thing.
notes.14:1: The Greek renders the mortal's condition as "full of wrath" (πλήρης ὀργῆς), using the same noun that refers to God's wrath in 14:13, rather than the Hebrew "full of turmoil."
notes.14:5: Continuing 14:4, the Greek adds "even if his life on the earth is one day," underscoring universal human impurity, and then shifts from third person ("by Him") to second person ("You appointed").
notes.14:9: The Greek renders the Hebrew word for "boughs" or "harvest" as "harvest" (θερισμόν), and in 14:8 places the dying stump "in rock" (ἐν πέτρᾳ) rather than "in dust."
notes.14:12: The unusual Greek clause "until heaven is not sewn together" (ἕως ἂν ὁ οὐρανὸς οὐ μὴ συνραφῇ) preserves the negation of the Hebrew "until the heavens are no more" while supplying a verb meaning to stitch or join together.
notes.14:14: Punctuated without an interrogative in this Greek text, the opening clause reads as a statement ("he will live") rather than a question, and "until I come into being again" (ἕως πάλιν γένωμαι) expresses renewal as renewed existence.
notes.15:2: Greek συνέσεως πνεύματος may mean "understanding of wind" or "understanding of spirit," and ἐνέπλησεν πόνον γαστρός (aorist, lit. "filled the pain of his belly") differs notably from the Masoretic Text ("fill his belly with the east wind").
notes.15:11: The Greek reads "You have been scourged for few of the things you have sinned" (ὀλίγα ὧν ἡμάρτηκας μεμαστίγωσαι), diverging sharply from the Masoretic Text ("Are the consolations of God too small for you?").
notes.15:23: Greek εἰς σῖτα γυψίν ("as food for vultures") reflects a reading of the Hebrew word for "where?" as "vulture/kite."
notes.15:27: Greek περιστόμιον literally denotes a "collar," "rim," or "border" (used here for a roll or fold of fat), likely chosen through an etymological link to the Hebrew word for "mouth."
notes.15:34: Greek μαρτύριον ("testimony") reflects Hebrew edut ("testimony") where the Masoretic Text reads adat ("company").
notes.16:6: Greek οὐκ ἀλγήσω τὸ τραῦμα literally states "I will not feel pain in the wound," contrasting with the Masoretic Text ("my pain is not assuaged").
notes.16:8: Greek τὸ ψεῦδός μου ("my falsehood") translates a Hebrew noun that can mean either "leanness" (as usually understood in the Masoretic Text) or "lying/deception."
notes.16:10: Greek ὀξεῖ ("with a sharp edge/point") and εἰς τὰ γόνατα ("on the knees") preserve a distinct Septuagint reading where the Masoretic Text has "with reproach they have struck my cheeks."
notes.16:16: The Greek reads ἡ γαστήρ μου ("My belly") rather than "My face" and simply σκιά ("a shadow") rather than "shadow of death" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.16:21: Greek ἔλεγχος denotes a legal "argument," "cross-examination," or "reproof," and the second clause places both "a son of man" and "his neighbor" in the dative (υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου τῷ πλησίον αὐτοῦ), rendering a comparison to pleading between neighbors.
notes.17:1: Greek πνεύματι φερόμενος means 'carried away by a wind' (or 'breath'/'spirit'), reflecting the Septuagint's distinctive poetic phrasing.
notes.17:5: An obscure Septuagint rendering: 'for the portion he will report evils' (τῇ μερίδι ἀναγγελεῖ κακίας), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'denounces friends for a share.'
notes.17:12: The Greek has first-person singular ἔθηκα ('I have turned'), unlike the third-person plural ('they turn') in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.18:9: The third-person singular verb κατισχύσει ('will strengthen') has an unexpressed subject, understood as God (compare 18:18) or an indefinite 'one'; 'thirsty ones' (διψῶντας) reflects the Septuagint's distinctive rendering.
notes.18:13: Literally 'branches of his feet' (κλῶνες ποδῶν), an unusual Septuagint expression for the extremities or limbs of his body.
notes.18:14: Greek αἰτίᾳ βασιλικῇ ('on a royal charge' or 'for a royal cause') is a notable Septuagint departure from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'king of terrors.'
notes.18:17: The Greek text lacks the negation ('no name') found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some later witnesses, reading literally 'there is a name for him on the face farther outside.'
notes.19:5: Greek ἔα δὲ ὅτι may be taken as the imperative of ἐάω ('yet let that be, for...') or as an exclamation ('ah, indeed...').
notes.19:7: The Septuagint reads γελῶ ὀνείδει ('I laugh at reproach'), diverging sharply from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'I cry out, Violence!'
notes.19:20: The Septuagint's 'my bones are held in teeth' (ἐν ὀδοῦσιν ἔχεται) leaves the possessor of the teeth unspecified and differs substantially from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.19:26: Accented as the aorist optative ἀναστήσαι, this expresses a wish ('May He raise up'); accented as the infinitive ἀναστῆσαι, it depends on μέλλων in 19:25 ('about to release me, to raise up on earth my skin').
notes.19:29: Greek ἐπικάλυμμα literally means 'covering,' 'cloak,' or 'pretext' (where the Hebrew has 'sword'), and ὕλη means 'wood,' 'material,' or 'substance.'
notes.20:1: The Greek text identifies Zophar as "the Minaean" (Μειναῖος), a South Arabian people, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the Naamathite."
notes.20:15: The Greek reads "an angel will drag it out of his house," differing from the Masoretic Text ("from his belly God will drive them out"); the masculine pronoun "it" (αὐτόν) may refer either to "wealth" (πλοῦτος) or to the ungodly man ("him").
notes.20:19: The Greek reads "of many powerful ones" (πολλῶν δυνατῶν), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to "the poor" (some scholars suspect an early Greek transcriptional shift from ἀδυνάτων, "weak ones").
notes.20:25: The Greek literally reads "may stars walk about in his dwellings" (ἄστρα δὲ ἐν διαίταις αὐτοῦ περιπατήσαισαν), diverging sharply from the Masoretic Text's imagery of a glittering point drawn from his gall.
notes.20:29: The Greek concludes with the distinctive divine title "the Overseer" (τοῦ ἐπισκόπου) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "God."
notes.21:2: Both here ("so that I may not have this comfort") and in 21:3 ("then you will not mock me"), the Greek introduces explicit negations absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.21:15: "The Sufficient One" translates Greek Ἱκανός, a distinctive Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew divine title Shaddai based on its traditional etymology ("sufficient").
notes.21:16: The Greek affirms that "their good things were in their hands" and adds that God "does not look upon the works of the ungodly," differing substantially from the Masoretic Text; likewise, 21:17 is framed as a statement ("Nevertheless...") rather than a question.
notes.21:22: The Greek reads "He Himself will judge murders" (φόνους), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "those on high."
notes.21:30: The Greek adds a singular pronoun in "a day of his wrath" (ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ) where the Masoretic Text has plural "wraths"; "his" most directly refers back to "the evil man" (either his own wrath or wrath against him), though some take it as referring to God's wrath.
notes.22:3: The Greek text reads aposes ("reject" or "push away," attested in Vaticanus and Sinaiticus); some manuscripts and modern editions read haploses ("make straight" or "plain").
notes.22:15: The Greek text reads andres dikaioi ("righteous men," as in Vaticanus and Sinaiticus), whereas other Greek witnesses read adikoi ("unrighteous men").
notes.22:20: Greek ei me (literally "if not") here represents an emphatic affirmative assertion ("surely") rather than a negative condition.
notes.22:22: The Greek text reads ekbale ("bring out" or "draw forth," attested in Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and Alexandrinus), where some editions emend to eklabe ("receive").
notes.22:24: Greek "Sophir" is the Septuagint proper name corresponding to Hebrew "Ophir." The Greek renders the verse with "in a rock" and "as a rock" where the Hebrew refers to gold of Ophir.
notes.23:2: Literally "out of my hand," an idiomatic Septuagint expression conveying that reproof is beyond Job's reach or control.
notes.23:4: The Greek verb emplesai is a third-person singular aorist optative ("He would fill"), though some manuscripts and editors read or interpret it as first-person ("I would fill").
notes.23:5: The Greek text reads iamata ("remedies" or "healings," attested in Vaticanus and Sinaiticus); other manuscripts and editions read rhemata ("words").
notes.23:15: Verse 14 of the Hebrew numbering is absent from the Greek text, while verse 15 preserves a double translation combining the Old Greek with a later Hexaplaric addition. Greek spoudazo and kataspoudazo here carry the Septuagint sense "dismay" or "alarm."
notes.24:5: The Septuagint differs markedly from the Hebrew here, reading "on my behalf" (hyper emou) and "bread was sweetened" (hedynthe, reflecting an alternate sense of the Hebrew root for "wilderness" or "sweet").
notes.24:14: Whereas the Hebrew depicts a murderer rising at dawn, the Septuagint depicts God knowing the works of the wicked and handing them over into darkness.
notes.24:17: Greek tarachos ("turmoil" or "terror") functions here as a heteroclite neuter accusative object of epignosetai ("he will recognize"); some manuscripts read the masculine plural accusative tarachous.
notes.24:21: Greek agynaios literally means "without a wife" or "wifeless," standing where the Hebrew text reads "widow."
notes.25:2: The Greek reads "prelude" (prooimion, also used in 27:1) and "the whole universe" (ten sympasan), reflecting a distinctive Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew terms for "dominion" and "peace."
notes.25:3: The Greek reads "respite for raiders" (parelkysis peiratais) and "ambush" (enedra), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("His troops" and "His light").
notes.25:5: Greek e is rendered as the asseverative particle "Indeed" rather than the conditional variant ei ("If").
notes.26:3: In 26:2-3 the Septuagint reverses the irony of the Hebrew by framing Bildad as aligning with the all-powerful and all-wise God; the middle verb symbebouleusai can mean "consulted" or "counseled."
notes.26:5: Greek gigantes ("giants") renders Hebrew rephaim (shades of the dead), and maiothesontai ("be brought forth") literally refers to delivery as by a midwife.
notes.26:11: Greek epetasthesan can derive either from petomai ("took flight") or from petannymi ("were spread wide"); the former aligns with the startled reaction in the parallel clause.
notes.26:12: Greek to ketos ("the sea monster") translates Hebrew Rahab, and the perfect passive estrotai ("has been laid low") makes the monster the grammatical subject.
notes.26:14: Greek ikmada logou ("a drop of a word") literally means a drop of moisture of a word, and hopote poiesei ("when He will make it") differs from the Hebrew ("who can understand").
notes.27:3: Greek pneuma theion ("divine spirit" or "divine breath," without the article) can also be capitalized as "the divine Spirit" in parallel with Job's life-breath.
notes.27:5: Because the Greek places gar ("for") after "until I die," that temporal clause concludes the first statement rather than introducing the second as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:8: The Septuagint reads "that he holds on? Trusting in the Lord, will he then be saved?", diverging markedly from the Hebrew ("when God takes away his soul").
notes.27:15: The Greek lacks the opening line found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("his survivors will be buried by pestilence") and reads "no one will have mercy on their widows" rather than "their widows will not weep."
notes.27:22: The grammatical subject continues from the scorching wind of 27:21, with cheiros autou literally "its hand" (idiomatically "its grasp"), though some take God as the implied subject.
notes.27:23: The Greek uses impersonal singular verbs (krotesei, syriei) alongside the plural pronoun auton ("their hands"), rendered with impersonal "they" for clarity in English.
notes.28:3: The Greek leaves the third-person subject of vv. 3 and 9-11 unexpressed. While the Hebrew imagery is commonly read of a human miner, the Septuagint wording ("set an order for darkness" in v. 3, and "displayed His own power to the light" in v. 11) presents these as actions of God.
notes.28:15: Greek synkleismos ("enclosure" or "something shut up") translates the rare Hebrew term for choice gold (segor) etymologically through the root "to shut/enclose."
notes.28:16: "Sophir" (Greek Sopheir) is the distinct Septuagint form of the place name Ophir.
notes.28:18: The Greek renders rare Hebrew gem terms literally or by transliteration: meteora ("lofty things") for coral, gabeis ("gabis," transliterated) for crystal, and ta esotata ("the innermost things") for pearls, while taking the Hebrew noun for "acquisition" as the imperative helkyson ("draw").
notes.28:25: The Greek text lacks a relative pronoun before "He made" (epoiesen, where some witnesses read ha epoiesen, "which He made"), and v. 26 retains the accusative plural phonas ("sounds") alongside "a way" (where some witnesses read the genitive "of sounds").
notes.29:1: Greek prooimion (literally "prelude" or "opening") is the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew term for a wisdom discourse or proverb (mashal).
notes.29:4: Greek epibrithon hodous ("pressing heavily upon the ways") and hylodes lian ("exceedingly wooded," v. 5) are distinctive Septuagint metaphors of abundance and vigor, diverging from the Hebrew ("in the days of my prime" and "when the Almighty was still with me").
notes.29:6: The Septuagint reads "my mountains flowed with milk," diverging from the Hebrew ("the rock poured out for me streams of oil").
notes.29:18: The Septuagint reads "My lifespan will grow old; like the trunk of a palm tree," where the Hebrew reads "I shall die in my nest" and refers to sand or a phoenix; in v. 19 the Greek similarly reads "harvest" (therismos) rather than "branches."
notes.29:20: The Greek reads literally "in his hand" (en cheiri autou) where the Hebrew has "in my hand"; ancient Greek interpreters sometimes understood "his hand" as referring to God.
notes.30:4: The Greek pairs halima ("saltwort", a salt-marsh plant) with alima (either a spelling variant or a wordplay suggesting hunger-staving food), while "by what resounds" (and "melodious ones" in 30:7) reflects the Septuagint rendering Hebrew words for bushes as terms of sound.
notes.30:20: Unlike the Hebrew, the Greek shifts here and in 30:21a to third-person plural verbs ("they stood and observed me, and they came upon me mercilessly") before returning to second-person singular address to God in 30:21b.
notes.30:24: In place of a difficult Hebrew line, the Septuagint expresses Job's explicit wish to lay violent hands on himself (cheirosasthai) or to ask someone else to do so for him.
notes.30:28: "Without a muzzle" (aneu phimou) is a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew has "without sun," and "sirens" in 30:29 is the standard Septuagint rendering of desert creatures where the Hebrew has "jackals."
notes.31:2: The Greek reads kai eti ("And yet") as a statement rather than the interrogative kai ti ("And what?") of some witnesses and the Hebrew. "The Sufficient One" (Hikanos) is the Septuagint's distinctive Greek title rendering Hebrew Shaddai.
notes.31:6: Rather than a wish ("let Him weigh me"), the Greek has a parenthetical perfect passive indicative (hestamai gar, "for I have been weighed"), expressing Job's confidence that he already stands tested.
notes.31:10: The Septuagint recasts the Hebrew imagery ("let my wife grind for another") as "may my wife also please another" and "may my little children be brought low."
notes.31:24: "In my dust" (eis choun mou) preserves the reading of the Greek text (suggesting buried gold or an early inner-Greek shift from ischyn, "strength," corresponding to Hebrew "confidence").
notes.31:35: In 31:35-37, the Septuagint recasts Job's call for a divine indictment into a counterfactual about a written debt-bond (syngraphen) held against a debtor (31:37): had he not feared the Lord's hand, he would have paraded and read it aloud instead of tearing it up and returning it without payment.
notes.32:1: The Greek reads 'his three friends' and 'righteous before them,' whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'these three men' and 'righteous in his own eyes.'
notes.32:2: The Greek adds 'of the land of Uz' (literally 'Ausitis') and reads 'before the Lord' where the Hebrew has 'rather than God.'
notes.32:7: Unlike the Hebrew ('Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom'), the Greek negates both clauses so that Elihu explicitly rejects age alone as the source of wisdom.
notes.32:17: Instead of continuing Elihu's direct speech as in the Hebrew, the Greek inserts a brief narrative formula introducing the next section of his discourse.
notes.32:22: The Greek literally reads 'admire persons' (an idiom for showing partiality) and concludes with 'moths will eat me too,' where the Hebrew has 'my Maker would soon take me away.'
notes.33:12: The Greek reads 'the One who is above mortals is eternal,' differing from the Hebrew 'God is greater than man.'
notes.33:14: The Greek verb is optative ('may speak') and leads directly into the dream imagery of verse 15 without the Hebrew clause 'and man does not perceive it.'
notes.33:20: Whereas the Hebrew describes the sick man's appetite as loathing choice food, the Greek states that he cannot accept grain food even while his soul desires food.
notes.33:23: The Greek speaks of 'a thousand death-bringing angels' unable to wound the sufferer and his confession of fault to another, diverging sharply from the Hebrew's 'angel, a mediator, one of a thousand.'
notes.33:24: The Greek simile 'like plaster on a wall' reflects a different sense of the Hebrew root for 'ransom' (which can also mean 'coat' or 'cover'), paired here with the renewal of the sufferer's body and bones.
notes.34:6: The Greek verb "has dealt falsely" (epseusato) is third-person singular referring to the Lord (unlike the first-person Hebrew), and "arrow" renders belos literally.
notes.34:8: The Greek distinctively prefixes "not having sinned nor acted ungodly" before "or having shared a way," softening Elihu's accusation against Job compared with the Hebrew text.
notes.34:10: In the Greek text, Elihu declares "Far be it from me" to act ungodly before the Lord, whereas the Hebrew reads "Far be it from God" to do wickedness.
notes.34:23: The Greek clause is elliptical (literally, "for He will not place upon a man any longer," without an expressed object) and lacks the second half of the verse present in the Hebrew.
notes.34:30: The Greek renders the participle positively as "making a hypocritical man king" (rather than negatively as in the Hebrew) and reads "because of the perversity of the people" (dyskolias).
notes.35:2: The Greek reads "Who are you that you said, 'I am righteous before the Lord'?" rather than the Hebrew "My righteousness is more than God's," and verse 3 is absent from the Greek text.
notes.35:10: The Greek reads "who appoints night watches" (phylakas nykterinas) where the Hebrew has "who gives songs in the night," and verse 11 links both phrases to the single participle "who distinguishes me."
notes.35:14: The Greek diverges substantially from the Hebrew here, affirming "and He will save me" and challenging Job to "be judged before Him, if you can praise Him as He is."
notes.35:16: The Greek verb barynei literally means "makes heavy," reflecting a different Hebrew root than the Masoretic "multiplies."
notes.36:3: The Greek reads "by my works" (ergois de mou), reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew from the Masoretic Text ("to my Maker").
notes.36:14: The Greek reads "wounded by angels" (titroskomene hypo angelon), differing markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("among the cult prostitutes").
notes.36:28: Greek palaiomata literally means "ancient/aged things" (also in 37:18, 21), an etymological rendering of the Hebrew word for "clouds/skies"; the final two sentences of this verse ("He appointed a season... from your body?") are a distinctive Septuagint expansion absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.36:30: The Greek text reads "the song" (he ode), a notable Septuagint reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "His light."
notes.36:33: The Greek syntax is highly compressed and reflects a literal rendering of an obscure underlying text, reading "His friend," "the Lord is a possession," and "concerning unrighteousness."
notes.37:4: Greek hybreos literally means "pride" or "arrogance," used here in the Septuagint to render the Hebrew term for "majesty" or "pride."
notes.37:12: Greek theeboulathoth is an untranslated transliteration of the Hebrew noun tahbulot, meaning "steering," "guidance," or "counsels."
notes.37:18: Greek horasis epichyseos literally means "appearance of an outpouring" (or "casting"), rendering the Hebrew imagery of a "molten mirror."
notes.37:24: The Greek reads positively that "the wise in heart will also fear Him," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text states that God does not regard any who are wise of heart.
notes.38:1: The Greek text opens with an explicit transition from Elihu's speech and states that the Lord spoke "through a whirlwind and clouds," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "out of the whirlwind" without mentioning Elihu or clouds.
notes.38:7: The Greek reads "all My angels" (pantes angeloi mou) where the Hebrew has "all the sons of God," and links the praise to the moment when the stars came into being.
notes.38:14: Unlike the Hebrew image of clay changed under a seal, the Greek depicts forming a living creature from clay and placing him on the earth able to speak, shifting from neuter zoon to masculine auton.
notes.38:32: "Mazuroth" transliterates the Hebrew astronomical term Mazzaroth, while "Hesperus" (the evening star) renders Greek Hesperon (matching 9:9; where Hebrew has the Bear), and "by its hair" literally renders epi komes autou.
notes.38:36: The Greek refers to women's wisdom of weaving and knowledge of embroidery, diverging markedly from the obscure Hebrew terms, variously understood as "inward parts" and "mind" or as "ibis" and "rooster."
notes.39:1: "Goat-stags" literally translates Greek tragelaphon (a wild mountain goat or ibex), preserving the Greek wordplay with elaphon ("deer") in the parallel clause.
notes.39:9: "Unicorn" literally translates Greek monokeros ("one-horned animal"), the Septuagint's regular rendering of the Hebrew wild ox (re'em).
notes.39:13: Part of the passage (vv. 13-18) supplied in Greek Job from Theodotion, this elliptical verse leaves the Hebrew nouns hasida ("stork") and nessa ("plumage") untransliterated and renders the Hebrew interrogative particle mechanically as "if" (ean).
notes.39:16: The abrupt phrase "so as not herself" literally translates Greek hoste me heauten, a cryptic Greek counterpart to the Hebrew "as though not hers."
notes.40:2: Greek Ikanou ("the Sufficient One") renders the Hebrew divine epithet Shaddai, while "turn aside judgment" reflects the Septuagint's distinct reading of the first clause.
notes.40:8: The Septuagint softens the reproach found in the Hebrew text, framing the Lord's dealing (Greek chrematizo) with Job as intended so that Job might appear righteous.
notes.40:15: The Septuagint translates Hebrew Behemoth literally as plural theria ("wild beasts") with a plural verb ("they eat"), before shifting to singular pronouns in verses 16-24.
notes.40:20: Greek tartaros ("Tartarus") is the classical name for the deepest underworld abyss, used by the Septuagint here and again in 41:24.
notes.40:32: The Greek text reads third-person epithesei ("one will lay"), whereas some witnesses read second-person epitheseis ("you will lay"). In the Septuagint, 40:25-32 introduces the dragon (Greek drakon, rendering Hebrew Leviathan) before chapter 41 begins.
notes.41:2: Greek "prepared for Me" (ἡτοίμασταί μοι) may also be understood as "prepared by Me."
notes.41:4: The second clause contains two accusatives in Greek (logon dynameos and ton ison autou) and is syntactically difficult; "concerning a word of power" renders the first phrase as an accusative of respect.
notes.41:18: The nouns "spear and breastplate" stand abruptly in the accusative case (dory kai thoraka) at the end of the clause, listing additional weapons that fail against the dragon.
notes.41:21: Greek sphyra here denotes hammers or mallets (a rare neuter plural form), and seismou pyrphorou literally means "shaking of a fire-bearer" (or "a fire-bearing earthquake").
notes.41:24: As in 40:20, the Septuagint uses Greek tartaros ("Tartarus") alongside abyssos ("abyss") to depict the deepest realm of the sea.
notes.42:6: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'repent in dust and ashes,' the Septuagint reads 'I held myself in contempt and wasted away, and I have regarded myself as earth and ashes.'
notes.42:8: The Greek idiom 'accept only his face' (introduced by a Hebraism for 'for only') means to show favor to Job alone. Unlike the Masoretic Text, the Greek has Job offer the burnt offerings, states 'I would have destroyed you,' and faults the friends for not speaking truthfully 'against My servant Job.'
notes.42:9: The Septuagint calls Zophar 'the Minaean' (and 'king of the Minaeans' in 42:17), referring to an Arabian people rather than the Masoretic Text's 'Naamathite.'
notes.42:14: The Septuagint renders the names of Job's three daughters into Greek as Day (Hemera), Cassia, and Horn of Amalthea (the Greek horn of plenty), corresponding to Hebrew Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch.
notes.42:17: Following the Septuagint lifespan in 42:16 (one hundred and seventy years after the affliction; two hundred and forty in all), this verse appends an ancient Greek postscript affirming Job's resurrection and identifying him with Jobab of Genesis 36:31-35. It preserves the Septuagint-distinct names Ennon, Balak (Hebrew Bela), Barad (Hebrew Bedad), and Getthaim (Hebrew Avith), and refers to Uz as Ausitis.
